clue.text: This angry argument repelled Germany

definitions.note: the clue refers to the very puzzle it sits in

parts.note: cross is a plain synonym for angry

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back, so the word for an argument is read backwards

parts.note: a row is a quarrel or argument

explanation.surface: Someone describes a heated quarrel in which Germany was pushed away.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the international vehicle code for Germany. The definition is the self-referential 'This': the thing you are solving.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue is part of a crossword, so 'this' points to the puzzle itself.

clue.text: Vote to support Charlie — poor old Charlie

indicators.note: in a down answer the lower part supports what sits above it, so the vote goes after the rest

parts.note: C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: poor here means badly made, so the letters of old are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a poll is a vote

explanation.surface: A cry of sympathy for a hapless old man called Charlie who has been outvoted.
explanation.walkthrough: A charlie is British slang for a silly person; a clodpoll is an archaic word for a blockhead.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal insults meaning a stupid or foolish person.

clue.text: Stop Ed Sheeran penning newspaper articles!

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the clue words hold the answer within them

parts.note: the letters run across the gap from the end of stop through Ed into the start of Sheeran

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea to stop the singer Ed Sheeran from writing for the papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' looks like writing, but here it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Op-eds are opinion pieces printed opposite a newspaper's editorial page.

clue.text: Very wide broadcast

definitions.note: a verb here: to scatter seed

parts.note: so is an intensifier like very
W is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a wide

explanation.surface: A description of a transmission that reaches a very large audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' first means scattering seed by hand, which is what sowing is.
explanation.definitionFit: To sow seed is to scatter it widely, the original farming sense of broadcast.

clue.text: Advanced, gold-plated blade

indicators.note: a plated item has a coating around it, so the gold surrounds the other letter

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A description of a fancy gilded sword or knife that has been put forward.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is gold in heraldry; A stands for advanced. The blade is the flat end of an oar.
explanation.definitionFit: An oar is a rowing implement, and its flat end is called the blade, so the word can stand for the whole.

clue.text: Members of stag party taking potentially lethal shots?

definitions.text: Members of stag party taking potentially lethal shots?

parts.words: Members of stag party taking potentially lethal shots
parts.note: reads as men on a pre-wedding night out downing dangerous drinks, but the party hunts stags and the shots are fired from guns

explanation.surface: Revellers on a stag night knocking back drinks that could do them real harm.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag party is a groom's night out before the wedding, and shots are strong drinks; the real party is out hunting stags with rifles.
explanation.definitionFit: People who stalk stags with guns are hunters of deer, and their shots can kill.

clue.text: Collude, occasionally dropping hint

indicators.note: taking only some letters at intervals, here every other one from the start

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of collude

explanation.surface: Someone who conspires every now and then and lets slip a tip-off.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue is a piece of information that helps solve a puzzle, much like a hint.

clue.text: Left American newspaper unfinished in NY airport

indicators.note: the word for the newspaper is left without its final letter

parts.note: the Guardian is a British national daily

explanation.surface: Someone leaves an incomplete American paper behind at a New York airport.
explanation.definitionFit: LaGuardia is one of New York City's main airports, in Queens.

clue.text: Waugh still lonely, empty inside

indicators.note: the emptied word goes within the word for still

parts.note: even, as in 'even now', means still

indicators.note: with its middle letters removed, leaving only the outer two

parts.note: lonely with its inner letters gone leaves just its first and last

explanation.surface: A writer named Waugh who remains solitary and hollow within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waugh' suggests Evelyn Waugh, the novelist, whose first name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Evelyn Waugh was the English novelist who wrote Brideshead Revisited; the answer is his first name.

clue.text: Used too much elaboration, having fingers to the bone?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: having worked one's fingers to the bone, toiling excessively

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense alludes to the idiom 'work your fingers to the bone'; the question mark flags the playful phrasing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes both art spoiled by excessive detail and a person exhausted by too much labour.

clue.text: Old King eaten by old English monster

indicators.note: something eaten is taken inside, so the king goes within old English

parts.note: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George

explanation.surface: An ancient king devoured by an old Englishman who turns out to be a monster.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of fairy tales, a classic monster.

clue.text: Industrial hand cleaner, fine and good, found in Devon/Cornwall region

indicators.note: with in, says the letter for good is found inside the region's letters
the letter for fine is placed inside the region's letters

parts.note: Devon and Cornwall lie in the south-west of England, giving SW plus area

explanation.surface: A product used by workmen to clean their hands, being sold in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: Swarfega is a British brand of green gel used to clean oily hands. The two letters go into separate gaps in the region.
explanation.definitionFit: Swarfega is a trade name for a heavy-duty gel that removes grease from mechanics' hands.

clue.text: According to Spooner, the majority of people criticise chap working with The Daily Mail

definitions.text: chap working with The Daily Mail

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first consonants are exchanged

parts.note: most people is the majority, and to pan is to criticise: MOST PAN, with its opening sounds swapped

explanation.surface: A survey suggesting most people dislike a man who works for the Daily Mail newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail is a British newspaper, but here 'daily mail' is just the letters delivered each day.
explanation.definitionFit: A postman delivers letters every day, so he works with the daily post.

clue.text: A rich art patron, Miss West: cold, rational upbringing

parts.note: Mae West was the American film star

indicators.note: in a down answer, bringing up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: sane means rational

explanation.surface: A wealthy patron of the arts described as a cool, sensible woman from a good background.
explanation.walkthrough: Maecenas was the wealthy friend of Augustus who supported Virgil and Horace; his name became a byword for a patron.
explanation.definitionFit: Maecenas, Roman sponsor of poets, gives his name to any generous benefactor of the arts.

clue.text: Russian mutt chewed flowers

indicators.note: something chewed is mangled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Russian dog has been gnawing at the garden plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasturtiums are garden plants with bright orange and yellow blooms.

clue.text: What number, roughly … why moan?

indicators.note: done roughly means done imprecisely, so the letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks for an approximate figure, then wonders why anyone would complain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' looks like it goes with 'What number' as in an estimate, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The question 'how many' asks for a quantity, the same as asking what number.

clue.text: 1A creators succeeded, becoming large property landlords

indicators.note: one letter turns into another, so the letter for succeeded is replaced by the letter for large

parts.note: 1 across is CROSSWORD, and crossword creators are setters

explanation.surface: Puzzle makers have done well and become big landlords.
explanation.walkthrough: S for succeeded is a genealogy abbreviation. Letters here are people who let property, not alphabet characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lets out a house or flat to tenants is a letter, that is, a landlord.

clue.text: Twist and Shout beginning to sell loads

indicators.note: to twist is to distort, so the following words have their letters rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: only the first letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of sell

explanation.surface: The Beatles' song Twist and Shout starting to sell in huge numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist and Shout' looks like the song title, but Twist is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Thousands is an informal way of saying a great many, just as loads is.

clue.text: Run into Auden, struggling poet

indicators.note: the letter for run goes inside the rearranged name
the letters of Auden are in difficulty and get jumbled

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Bumping into W. H. Auden, a poet having a hard time.
explanation.walkthrough: Auden looks like the poet in question, but the answer is the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Neruda was a Chilean poet who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.

clue.text: Rum? Just a little 'un

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small measure of spirits such as rum

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' could be the adjective meaning odd, but it is the drink, and a tot is a small dram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot is both a small serving of liquor and a very young child.

clue.text: Canute astride old command horse

indicators.note: sitting astride something means having one part on each side, so the king's name wraps the command

parts.note: Cnut is the older spelling of King Canute's name
hest is an archaic word for a command, as in behest

explanation.surface: King Canute sits astride a horse while giving an old-fashioned order.
explanation.definitionFit: A chestnut is a horse with a reddish-brown coat.

clue.text: Middle-of-the-road French water colourist

parts.note: MOR is the radio industry abbreviation for middle-of-the-road music
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: A painter of watercolours whose style is unadventurous and French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water colourist' reads as one phrase, but the water belongs with French.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustave Moreau was a French Symbolist painter noted for rich, jewel-like colour.

clue.text: Lid attachment secured in flash sale yesterday sent back

indicators.note: the held letters are read in reverse order
the answer is held within the run of clue words

parts.note: the letters run from the end of flash through sale into the start of yesterday

explanation.surface: Something you fix to a lid was bought in yesterday's quick sale and then returned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lid' sounds like a container's top, but it is the eyelid.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelash grows from the edge of the eyelid, so it is attached to a lid.

clue.text: A coming commercial opening

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
a vent is an opening for air

explanation.surface: A notice that an advertisement launch is on the way.
explanation.definitionFit: An advent is an arrival or coming, from the Latin for 'to come'.

clue.text: Two notes? Barely sufficient counterpoint added to melody

parts.note: D and E are two notes of the scale
scant means barely enough

explanation.surface: A music teacher asks whether just two notes provide enough harmony against the tune.
explanation.definitionFit: A descant is an independent counter-melody sung or played above the main tune.

clue.text: Bandages cut initially from samples of cloth

indicators.note: taken from means removed out of the word for the samples

parts.note: swatches are small pieces of fabric shown as samples

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word cut is used

parts.note: the first letter of cut

explanation.surface: Bandages are cut from fabric samples at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' seems to be the action of the bandager, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To swathe is to wrap in cloth, so as a verb swathes means wraps up, like bandages.

clue.text: Ancient 4 buried in the outskirts of Henley

indicators.note: the answer to 4 is placed inside the other letters
only the outermost letters of the word, its first and last

parts.note: the first and last letters of Henley
4 down is OAR

explanation.surface: An old oar lies buried on the edge of Henley, the Thames rowing town.
explanation.walkthrough: Henley-on-Thames hosts a famous rowing regatta, which suits the oar.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoary means grey with age and so, by extension, very old.

clue.text: Italian hothead Alighieri backed taking day off

indicators.note: taking a letter off means removing it from the reversed name
with taking, says the letter for day comes away
the poet's name is read backwards

parts.note: Dante Alighieri, the Italian poet

explanation.surface: An Italian with a fiery temper, Dante, took a day's holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hothead' sounds like an angry person, but it is a volcano, whose head is hot.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the active volcano in Sicily, a mountain with a fiery summit.

clue.text: Blur, Pulp in rare work of genius

indicators.note: to blur is to smudge, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Britpop bands Blur and Pulp at their rare best.
explanation.walkthrough: Blur and Pulp look like two band names; Blur is the anagram signal. Purple Rain is Prince's 1984 album.
explanation.definitionFit: Purple Rain, the album and film by Prince, is widely hailed as a masterpiece.

clue.text: Constant energy food

parts.note: pi is the mathematical constant

explanation.surface: Endless energy food.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie is a baked dish of pastry with a filling, a common foodstuff.

clue.text: Lug out of Le Havre regularly

indicators.note: letters taken at regular intervals, every second one

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of Le Havre

explanation.surface: Hauling something out of the French port of Le Havre on a routine basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lug' reads as a verb for carrying, but it is the British informal noun for an ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Lug, or lughole, is British slang for an ear.

clue.text: The Apprentice: Sugar knows the beginners aren't up to it!

definitions.text: The Apprentice: Sugar knows the beginners aren't up to it!

indicators.note: the beginnings of words, so the first letter of each is taken

parts.note: the first letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Lord Sugar on The Apprentice knows the novice candidates can't cope.
explanation.walkthrough: The Apprentice is a TV business contest hosted in Britain by Alan Sugar, where teams are set a weekly task they often fail.
explanation.definitionFit: On The Apprentice, contestants each week face a task, the job the novices aren't up to.

clue.text: Drunken Sybarite downing whiskey will attest to its powers

indicators.note: drinking something takes it inside, so the letter goes into the word
drunk means unsteady, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A tipsy pleasure-seeker swears by whiskey's virtues after knocking it back.
explanation.definitionFit: To swear by something is to vouch confidently for its effectiveness.
